title: Even inside your home, some hours are private.
subtitle: Three times of rest, and teaching children to knock
then: Earlier the surah taught how strangers ask to enter. Ibn Kathir notes these verses turn to {idea}those who live in the same house,{/idea} like young children and servants. Outside the three times, they move about freely, since they {reward}go around the house serving and helping.{/reward} Ibn Abbas lamented that {trap}most people had stopped following it.{/trap}
now: Your six-year-old bursts into your room at 6am, every day. You laugh, but you also wish they knocked. This verse gives the family {idea}a gentle shared rhythm:{/idea} three times when even little ones ask first. It is not coldness. It is teaching respect at home.
old: Little children do not need to learn privacy yet.
new: Allah teaches even young children to respect the private hours of a home.
try: Teach a child at home, kindly, to knock and wait at your door at one of these three times.

title: When children grow up, their manners grow up too.
subtitle: Reaching maturity means asking like the adults do
then: Ibn Kathir explains that once children who used to ask at the three times reach puberty, {idea}they ask permission as the adults before them did,{/idea} not only at those times. Allah ends again: this is how He makes the verses clear, and He is {reward}Knowing and Wise.{/reward}
now: Your son is suddenly taller than you. He wants his own room, his own rules, his own phone password. This verse adds the other half of growing up: {idea}he knocks, too.{/idea} Respect for privacy flows both ways once a child becomes an adult.
old: Growing up means getting more rights.
new: Growing up means taking on the manners of adults, including asking first.
try: If you have a teenager, talk with them today about knocking and privacy, both ways.

title: An ease is given, and restraint is still called better.
subtitle: Older women, ease, and the choice of modesty
then: Ibn Kathir notes this speaks of women past childbearing who no longer seek marriage. Allah eases things for them, without any {trap}display of adornment.{/trap} Then He adds that {idea}to refrain is better for them,{/idea} even though the ease is there. The verse closes: Allah is Hearing and Knowing.
now: Your grandmother could choose the easier option and nobody would blame her. She still holds to the extra step, quietly, because she loves it. This verse honors that: {idea}between allowed and better is a space for love.{/idea} Many good deeds live in that space.
old: If something is allowed, there is no reason to do more.
new: Allah gives ease and still points to what is better, leaving room for love.
try: Choose one thing today where you could take the easy way, and take the better one instead, just for Allah.

title: Eat together, eat with the disabled, and greet as you enter.
subtitle: Removing awkwardness from shared meals
then: Sa'id bin Jubayr said people felt awkward eating with the blind, lame or sick, {trap}fearing they might be unfair to them.{/trap} Ad-Dahhak said some were too proud. Mujahid said the disabled felt ashamed being taken to others' homes. Allah removed it all. A man told the Prophet ﷺ they ate but felt unsatisfied, and he said: {reward}eat together and mention Allah's name.{/reward}
now: Your uncle in a wheelchair always ends up eating in another room "so he is comfortable." The friend who lives alone eats standing at the counter. This verse pulls the chairs back to the table. {reward}Eat together.{/reward} And when you walk into your own home tonight, say salaam, even if the house is empty.
old: It is easier for everyone if some people eat separately.
new: Allah removes the awkwardness; blessing is in eating together and greeting with peace.
try: Invite someone who usually eats alone to share a meal with you this week. Say salaam when you enter.

title: True believers ask before they leave.
subtitle: Manners for leaving a shared gathering
then: Ibn Kathir explains that just as Allah taught them to ask permission to enter, He taught them to {idea}ask permission to leave{/idea} when gathered with the Prophet ﷺ for something shared, like Friday prayer or a consultation. He cites the hadith: give salaam when you join a gathering and when you leave, {idea}the first is not more important than the last.{/idea}
now: The community meeting is running long. You have somewhere to be. You could just quietly vanish. Or you could catch the organizer's eye, say "I need to head off, salaam." This verse makes that small moment {idea}a sign of real faith,{/idea} and a reason for prayers on your behalf.
old: Leaving early quietly is more polite than interrupting.
new: Asking and greeting when I leave a shared matter is part of real faith.
try: The next time you leave a gathering, say salaam on your way out.

title: He is holding you back from the fire. Do not slip away.
subtitle: Honoring the Messenger ﷺ and his way
then: Ibn Abbas said people used to call him O Muhammad, and Allah taught them to say {idea}O Messenger of Allah.{/idea} Muqatil said some hypocrites would {trap}hide behind others and sneak out{/trap} during the Friday sermon. Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet's ﷺ parable: {reward}I am holding you by your waist, away from the fire,{/reward} and you overwhelm me and rush in.
now: Moths circle a streetlight at night and keep throwing themselves at it. You watch from your balcony and wonder why. Then you think of the habits you keep flying back to, after being warned. {reward}Someone is still holding your waist.{/reward} The Sunnah is his hand. Do not slip out of it.
old: The Sunnah is a set of nice extras.
new: The Prophet's ﷺ way is a hand pulling me back from harm.
try: Pick one Sunnah you have dropped and bring it back today, with love for the one who taught it.

title: He already knows where you stand.
subtitle: The surah closes with Allah's knowledge of everything
then: Ibn Kathir closes the surah by noting that Allah knows what His servants do {idea}in secret and in the open,{/idea} and not one speck is hidden from Him. On the Day of return, He will inform each person of what they did, {trap}major and minor.{/trap} He compares it to a book that leaves out nothing small or big.
now: A whole surah about rumors, homes, eyes, doors, meals and light. It all ends here: {idea}Allah knows where you stand.{/idea} Not where you say you stand. Not where your feed says. The real place. That is scary only until you remember He also knows every effort you made to turn back.
old: No one really knows what I am going through.
new: Allah knows exactly where I stand, and every step I take toward Him.
try: Tonight, sit for two minutes and tell Allah honestly where you stand. He already knows.
